d4d7b83174cbe702.text: Anneke in data protection wrote to our channel this morning. No greeting, no exclamation marks. When Anneke skips the exclamation marks, I put my coffee down.

3ca82ca83be14b38.text: A customer has asked us, in writing, where the data in one support ticket was processed. Their contract names a region, and Anneke has to sign the reply this week.

52f9ebc0dbb6b9dc.text: Our first instinct was to send her the routing rules. But a rule only says what we meant to happen. Anneke wants to see what actually happened to one real request.

0ee038759cedb2e2.text: Then Tomasz remembered something awkward. Our EU route isn't a straight line to its provider. Something sits in the middle, and he never wrote down what.

1b3e01c003cd38e9.text: Here's the good news. Every request through our gateway leaves a trace, a record from each service that touched it. And the gateway keeps its own log of every call it sends.

227aed034ad9336c.text: So that's your job today. Send real requests through our regional aliases, open their traces, and read what each hop says about itself. Then hold it up against what we declared.

e7555751f3c6241f.text: Pin down three things. Where a request through the US alias really ended up. How many services touched one through the EU alias, gateway included. And whether every region tag matches what we declared.

5d99d0766af563f4.text: Anneke will ask how you know. So answer from what happened, not from what was meant to happen. Over to you.
